Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Advanced Movement

Advanced Movement Mechanics & Character Controllers

Practical guide to converting pawns into characters and wiring physics-aware movement in C++.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson

Convert a pawn to ACharacter, configure movement, and implement Jump and Sprint with reliable resets.

Why it matters

Character components save time and avoid fragile custom physics when building humanoid players and NPCs.

APawn vs ACharacter
APawn is minimal. ACharacter includes capsule and movement component suitable for bipedal actors.
Movement Component
Handles gravity, walking, jumping, and network prediction out of the box.
Controller & Possession
APlayerController possesses the pawn and mediates input and high-level logic like HUD and menus.
Concept Map
Capsule → MovementComponent → Controller → InputActions
Capsule Collision
Defines physical bounds used by CharacterMovement to handle stepping and slope detection.
Movement Component
Manages gravity, jumping, falling and network prediction—so you rarely need manual delta-time multipliers in Move().
Explore Key Topics
Choosing ACharacter when you need built-in walking, jumping, and network-safe movement.
Configuring MaxWalkSpeed, JumpZVelocity, and bOrientRotationToMovement for responsive controls.
Binding Jump and Sprint actions using the Enhanced Input system and resetting speeds safely.

screens.title: APawn vs ACharacter
screens.narratorSegment: APawn is the minimal, flexible base class for anything that can be possessed. It provides the possession and input hooks but does not assume how movement should work. That makes APawn ideal for vehicles, flying drones, or camera rigs where movement logic is special and the developer wants full control. ACharacter, by contrast, is an APawn subclass built for humanoid-style movement. It contains a UCapsuleComponent for collision and a UCharacterMovementComponent that implements walking, falling, gravity, stepping up small obstacles, and network prediction. Use ACharacter when your actor needs to walk, jump, crouch or interact with uneven geometry; it saves vast effort compared to implementing these features on a raw APawn. A common misconception is that ACharacter limits flexibility; in practice you can still extend or replace parts, and the movement component is configurable for a wide range of behaviors. Concrete example: for a player-controlled humanoid with third-person camera you should choose ACharacter — the movement component handles delta-time, gravity, and step-up so AddMovementInput remains simple. For a spaceship that uses thrust and free rotation, APawn is the right choice because character-specific logic would conflict with flight physics. Reflect: which actors in your project need the built-in character behaviors and which need a bespoke movement system?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › APawn vs ACharacter
APawn
Minimal possession base. Use when you need full control over movement logic: vehicles, spaceships, and flying drones.
Pros: Flexible, lightweight, no character assumptions.
Cons: You must implement collision response, gravity, and stepping if needed.
Example: A drivable spaceship with thrust-based movement.
ACharacter
Includes UCapsuleComponent and UCharacterMovementComponent to provide walking, jumping, and network-friendly movement for humanoid actors.
Pros: Pre-built physics-aware movement, slope and step handling, jump helpers, and prediction.
Cons: Slight overhead and some constraints if you need radically different physics.
Example: Player character in a third-person game that walks, jumps and crouches.
Check your understanding
If your actor needs built-in step-up, slope behavior and network prediction for humanoid movement, choose ACharacter. If movement is entirely custom, choose APawn.

screens.title: UCharacterMovementComponent Essentials
screens.narratorSegment: The UCharacterMovementComponent is the primary workhorse for biped movement. It handles gravity, falling, walking, jumping, stepping up onto obstacles, and network prediction. Important properties include MaxWalkSpeed which caps horizontal velocity; JumpZVelocity which controls vertical impulse on jump; AirControl which affects how much directional control the player has while airborne; BrakingDecelerationWalking which determines how quickly the character slows when input stops; and bOrientRotationToMovement which, when true, makes the mesh face the current movement direction. These properties are configured typically in the character constructor, and they dramatically change player feel. A common misconception is that movement feels 'laggy' because of input binding; often the issue is a low MaxWalkSpeed, too much braking, or incorrect AirControl settings. Another key detail: you should not multiply movement input by delta time when using AddMovementInput on a character — the movement component applies time scaling internally. Concrete example: setting JumpZVelocity to 600 and AirControl to 0.2 produces a jump with limited mid-air steering, suitable for platforming with predictable arcs. Always test combinations of these properties together — a high MaxWalkSpeed combined with low BrakingDecelerationWalking will feel slippery. Takeaway: tune these knobs iteratively and record DefaultWalkSpeed so sprinting can revert reliably.

keyIdea.title: Tuning knobs
keyIdea.text: MaxWalkSpeed, JumpZVelocity, AirControl, and braking are the primary properties to tune movement feel and stability.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Movement Component
Key properties
MaxWalkSpeed
Caps horizontal movement speed. Used when switching to sprint by multiplying a stored default.
JumpZVelocity
Controls the vertical impulse applied on Jump(). Larger values produce higher arcs.
AirControl
Amount of directional control while airborne. Low values make jumps predictable; high values allow steering.
BrakingDecelerationWalking
How quickly you come to a stop when input ceases; affects responsiveness and sliding.
Practical tuning tips
  • Set DefaultWalkSpeed in BeginPlay for safe sprint resets.
  • Do not multiply AddMovementInput by delta time; the movement component handles time scaling.
  • Test combinations: speed, braking, and air control interact and change feel.
Key Takeaway

Tune movement component properties iteratively and store defaults to make temporary changes like sprinting reversible and predictable.

screens.title: Creating AMyPlayerCharacter — Header
screens.narratorSegment: When you create AMyPlayerCharacter from the Character base, add UInputAction pointers and function declarations for movement, look, jumping and sprinting. The header typically stores references to your input mapping context and the digital actions for Jump and Sprint. Also add a SprintSpeedMultiplier and a DefaultWalkSpeed field so you can modify MaxWalkSpeed temporarily and revert it. Concretely, declare Move and Look handlers that accept the Enhanced Input value and JumpStarted, JumpCompleted, SprintStarted, SprintCompleted functions for digital events. This separation lets you bind started and completed triggers so sprint ends when the key is released. One misconception to avoid: do not store MaxWalkSpeed in the constructor as the ultimate default; store it in BeginPlay because defaults can change through Blueprints or data assets. Header snippet
// In AMyPlayerCharacter.h
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "GameFramework/Character.h"
#include "InputActionValue.h"
#include "MyPlayerCharacter.generated.h"

UCLASS()
class YOURGAME_API AMyPlayerCharacter : public ACharacter
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    AMyPlayerCharacter();

protected:
    virtual void BeginPlay() override;
    virtual void SetupPlayerInputComponent(UInputComponent* PlayerInputComponent) override;

    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadOnly, Category = "Input")
    UInputMappingContext* PlayerInputMappingContext;

    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadOnly, Category = "Input")
    UInputAction* MoveAction;

    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadOnly, Category = "Input")
    UInputAction* LookAction;

    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadOnly, Category = "Input")
    UInputAction* JumpAction; // New action for jumping

    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadOnly, Category = "Input")
    UInputAction* SprintAction; // New action for sprinting

    void Move(const FInputActionValue& Value);
    void Look(const FInputActionValue& Value);
    void JumpStarted(const FInputActionValue& Value);
    void JumpCompleted(const FInputActionValue& Value);
    void SprintStarted(const FInputActionValue& Value);
    void SprintCompleted(const FInputActionValue& Value);

    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadOnly, Category = "Movement")
    float SprintSpeedMultiplier = 1.5f; // How much faster to sprint
    float DefaultWalkSpeed; // To store original walk speed
};
Tip: mark input pointers with EditAnywhere so you can assign input assets in the Blueprint defaults view after compiling.
Supporting notes
  • Use BeginPlay to store DefaultWalkSpeed because defaults may be modified in editor.
  • Declare both Started and Completed handlers for digital actions to ensure proper resets.
Check

Do you have both JumpAction and SprintAction declared and the SprintSpeedMultiplier available to modify MaxWalkSpeed?

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Constructor & Movement
Constructor snippet
AMyPlayerCharacter::AMyPlayerCharacter()
{
    PrimaryActorTick.bCanEverTick = true;

    // Set size for collision capsule
    GetCapsuleComponent()->InitCapsuleSize(42.f, 96.0f);

    // Don't rotate when the controller rotates. Let that just affect the camera.
    bUseControllerRotationPitch = false;
    bUseControllerRotationYaw = false;
    bUseControllerRotationRoll = false;

    // Configure character movement
    GetCharacterMovement()->bOrientRotationToMovement = true;
    GetCharacterMovement()->RotationRate = FRotator(0.0f, 540.0f, 0.0f);
    GetCharacterMovement()->JumpZVelocity = 600.f;
    GetCharacterMovement()->AirControl = 0.2f;
    GetCharacterMovement()->MaxWalkSpeed = 600.f;
    GetCharacterMovement()->MinAnalogWalkSpeed = 20.f;
    GetCharacterMovement()->BrakingDecelerationWalking = 2000.f;

    // Camera boom and follow camera setup omitted for brevity
}
Note: after compilation, set camera and spring arm defaults in Blueprint if you need designer-driven adjustments.
Common pitfall
If you forget to set bUseControllerRotationYaw to false while also using bOrientRotationToMovement, the character will receive conflicting rotation and the mesh will jitter. Fix this in the constructor.
Pro tip

Tune RotationRate to get responsive turns without snapping. Higher rotation rate = faster facing changes.

screens.title: Movement Input & AddMovementInput
screens.narratorSegment: Movement input flows from your Enhanced Input Move action into a Move handler that extracts a two-dimensional vector. In a typical third-person setup you read the controller rotation, derive a yaw-only rotation and then compute forward and right vectors. Pass the input scale to AddMovementInput with the world direction — do not multiply by delta time for ACharacter because the movement component manages timing internally. For example, call AddMovementInput(ForwardDirection, MovementVector. Y) and AddMovementInput(RightDirection, MovementVector. X). This keeps input handling frame-independent and leverages built-in movement replication. A frequent misconception is to think AddMovementInput requires delta-time; applying it manually leads to double time-scaling and inconsistent speeds. Concrete example: when holding forward you’ll see the character accelerate to MaxWalkSpeed governed by the movement component. If you need analog input smoothing, do it on the input value before calling AddMovementInput, but avoid altering the movement component’s internal timing. Finally, confirm that bOrientRotationToMovement is set if you want the mesh to face movement direction — otherwise you might set controller yaw instead. Movement Input & AddMovementInput means let addmovementinput handle time-scaling; supply directional vectors and raw input scales only.. In practical terms, how movement vectors become charactermovement behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Move() Behavior
Process
1. Read FVector2D from Enhanced Input Move action.
2. Get controller yaw and compute ForwardDirection and RightDirection.
3. Call AddMovementInput(ForwardDirection, MovementVector.Y) and AddMovementInput(RightDirection, MovementVector.X).
4. Rely on UCharacterMovementComponent for delta-time scaling and replication.
Example snippet
void AMyPlayerCharacter::Move(const FInputActionValue& Value)
{
    FVector2D MovementVector = Value.Get<FVector2D>();
    if (Controller != nullptr)
    {
        const FRotator Rotation = Controller->GetControlRotation();
        const FRotator YawRotation(0, Rotation.Yaw, 0);

        const FVector ForwardDirection = FRotationMatrix(YawRotation).GetUnitAxis(EAxis::X);
        const FVector RightDirection = FRotationMatrix(YawRotation).GetUnitAxis(EAxis::Y);

        AddMovementInput(ForwardDirection, MovementVector.Y);
        AddMovementInput(RightDirection, MovementVector.X);
    }
}
Check: remove any * GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds() multipliers; they are not needed for characters.

screens.title: Jumping: Jump() and StopJumping()
screens.narratorSegment: ACharacter provides Jump() and StopJumping() as built-in semantics for initiating and ending a jump. Bind your JumpAction such that the started trigger calls Jump(), and the completed trigger calls StopJumping(). This ensures the character receives the expected vertical impulse and any hold-to-jump behavior is correctly interpreted by the movement component. screens.title: Sprinting: Safe MaxWalkSpeed Management
screens.narratorSegment: Sprinting is commonly implemented by multiplying the character's default MaxWalkSpeed when the sprint key is held and restoring it when released. Another pitfall is modifying MaxWalkSpeed in multiple places without a clear owner for the value; prefer a single source of truth and use setters if necessary. Always test sprint on both client and server. Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Input Binding
Binding example
void AMyPlayerCharacter::SetupPlayerInputComponent(UInputComponent* PlayerInputComponent)
{
    Super::SetupPlayerInputComponent(PlayerInputComponent);

    if (UEnhancedInputComponent* EnhancedInputComponent = Cast<UEnhancedInputComponent>(PlayerInputComponent))
    {
        if (MoveAction) { EnhancedInputComponent->BindAction(MoveAction, ETriggerEvent::Triggered, this, &AMyPlayerCharacter::Move); }
        if (LookAction) { EnhancedInputComponent->BindAction(LookAction, ETriggerEvent::Triggered, this, &AMyPlayerCharacter::Look); }

        if (JumpAction)
        {
            EnhancedInputComponent->BindAction(JumpAction, ETriggerEvent::Started, this, &AMyPlayerCharacter::JumpStarted);
            EnhancedInputComponent->BindAction(JumpAction, ETriggerEvent::Completed, this, &AMyPlayerCharacter::JumpCompleted);
        }

        if (SprintAction)
        {
            EnhancedInputComponent->BindAction(SprintAction, ETriggerEvent::Started, this, &AMyPlayerCharacter::SprintStarted);
            EnhancedInputComponent->BindAction(SprintAction, ETriggerEvent::Completed, this, &AMyPlayerCharacter::SprintCompleted);
        }
    }
}
Assignment tips
  • After compiling, assign IMC_Player and IA_* assets to the Blueprint defaults.
  • Ensure the PlayerController adds the mapping context so actions fire.

screens.title: APlayerController & Possession
screens.narratorSegment: The APlayerController acts as the player's brain: it is created for each human player and then possesses a pawn or character to link input to the actor's body. Possession ties the controller to a pawn and routes input events to that pawn's input component, which is why SetupPlayerInputComponent on the pawn/character matters. APlayerController also handles higher-level responsibilities such as HUD management, pausing, and menu navigation — tasks that shouldn't live in the character class. A common misconception is to put UI and movement logic in the same class; keeping HUD and possession in the controller preserves separation of concerns. When converting a pawn to ACharacter, ensure your GameMode's default pawn is updated or your PlayerController possesses the new character instance. In multiplayer, possession events may happen on server and client at different times; test possession flows and confirm that input mapping contexts are added to the correct controller, so input actions are delivered as expected. Question to consider: when your player joins, does the controller add the mapping context and immediately possess the character, or do you configure the pawn as default in the GameMode to simplify the startup sequence?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Controller & Possession
Role of APlayerController
The controller is responsible for possessing a pawn or character and routing input. It also manages HUD, menus, and other player-scoped systems that are independent of a specific character instance.
Possession flow
  1. PlayerController is created when a player joins.
  2. Controller possesses a pawn/character either via GameMode default pawn or manual possession.
  3. Input mapping contexts are added to the controller so the pawn receives Enhanced Input events.
Practical note
Keep HUD and high-level game logic in the controller. Movement and body behavior belong to the pawn/character for cleaner, testable code.

screens.title: Common Mistakes & Multiplayer Notes
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few recurring mistakes developers make when implementing character movement. First, enabling both bUseControllerRotationYaw and bOrientRotationToMovement creates a conflict: the character attempts to match controller yaw while also orienting to movement, which results in jerky rotation. Fix this by setting bUseControllerRotationYaw to false when bOrientRotationToMovement is true. Second, not storing DefaultWalkSpeed before modifying MaxWalkSpeed for sprinting causes SprintCompleted to fail to restore the correct speed. Always capture the default in BeginPlay. Third, multiplying AddMovementInput by delta time is unnecessary and will lead to inconsistent movement because the CharacterMovementComponent already applies delta-time scaling. In multiplayer, movement is sensitive to latency; UCharacterMovementComponent includes prediction, but custom movement logic can break reconciliation. Test movement on both client and server and avoid client-only authoritative changes to critical movement properties. Finally, when debugging, reproduce the issue in a controlled map with a simple character and toggle properties like JumpZVelocity and AirControl to isolate the cause. These checks will save hours of intermittent bugs during testing. Common Mistakes & Multiplayer Notes means turn off controller yaw when orienting to movement, store defaults for sprint, and avoid manual delta-time multiplication; test multiplayer.. In practical terms, avoid rotation conflicts and sprint persistence; test networked movement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Common mistakes
  • Conflict between bUseControllerRotationYaw and bOrientRotationToMovement — set yaw false when orienting to movement.

Toggle suspected properties, reproduce in a minimal map, and validate BeginPlay initialization order. Use logging to confirm SprintCompleted is executed on key release.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will move from a simple pawn to a full-featured character that understands gravity, jumping, and sprinting. You will learn when to prefer ACharacter over APawn, how the UCharacterMovementComponent provides physics-aware movement, and how the APlayerController ties player input to the character body. I’ll walk you through creating a C++ AMyPlayerCharacter, configuring its constructor for sensible defaults, and binding jump and sprint input actions so the movement code behaves predictably. We will also look at common mistakes that produce jerky rotation or broken sprint resets and how to test movement in multiplayer. By the end you should be comfortable converting a pawn-based player to a character, tuning MaxWalkSpeed and JumpZVelocity, and ensuring the controller and movement component interact correctly during possession. To ground this, you’ll see concrete code snippets used in a typical third-person setup and a short checklist for testing on both client and server. Think about your current player class: would it be simpler to inherit APawn, or will ACharacter save time and bugs for humanoid movement?

These objectives prepare you to build robust humanoid movement in C++. First, you will be able to differentiate APawn from ACharacter and decide which base class makes your life easier. I’ll show the practical tradeoffs so your choice avoids costly rewrites. Second, you will use the UCharacterMovementComponent to implement physics-aware movement: you’ll learn which properties to tune and why they matter for slope handling, jumping, and step-ups. Third, you will implement common mechanics such as jump and sprint by binding Enhanced Input actions and using ACharacter’s built-in Jump and StopJumping functions, along with safe MaxWalkSpeed modifications. Finally, you will understand the role of APlayerController for possession and high-level game logic, and how it connects input to the pawn. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual hint so you can recall the right decision in the editor. Understanding these objectives reduces bugs and speeds up multiplayer testing, since movement-related desynchronization is one of the most common problems in networked games.

This second objectives slide focuses on actionable workflows. You will create a C++ AMyPlayerCharacter from the Character parent and wire its constructor to initialize the capsule, camera boom and follow camera so the actor behaves as a third-person player. You will then add input properties for Move, Look, Jump and Sprint, and implement SetupPlayerInputComponent to bind started and completed events for jump and sprint. Next, you'll store DefaultWalkSpeed in BeginPlay so sprint resets are reliable. Finally, you will test in-editor: assign input assets, place the character in the level, and set it as the default pawn in your GameMode. These steps are deliberately sequential; missing one — for example failing to store DefaultWalkSpeed — is a frequent cause of persistent sprint bugs. The goal is that after following these steps you can reproduce the same behavior shown in the sample code and confirm the character rotates toward movement while the camera remains controller-driven.

APawn is the minimal, flexible base class for anything that can be possessed. It provides the possession and input hooks but does not assume how movement should work. That makes APawn ideal for vehicles, flying drones, or camera rigs where movement logic is special and the developer wants full control. ACharacter, by contrast, is an APawn subclass built for humanoid-style movement. It contains a UCapsuleComponent for collision and a UCharacterMovementComponent that implements walking, falling, gravity, stepping up small obstacles, and network prediction. Use ACharacter when your actor needs to walk, jump, crouch or interact with uneven geometry; it saves vast effort compared to implementing these features on a raw APawn. A common misconception is that ACharacter limits flexibility; in practice you can still extend or replace parts, and the movement component is configurable for a wide range of behaviors. Concrete example: for a player-controlled humanoid with third-person camera you should choose ACharacter — the movement component handles delta-time, gravity, and step-up so AddMovementInput remains simple. For a spaceship that uses thrust and free rotation, APawn is the right choice because character-specific logic would conflict with flight physics. Reflect: which actors in your project need the built-in character behaviors and which need a bespoke movement system?

The UCharacterMovementComponent is the primary workhorse for biped movement. It handles gravity, falling, walking, jumping, stepping up onto obstacles, and network prediction. Important properties include MaxWalkSpeed which caps horizontal velocity; JumpZVelocity which controls vertical impulse on jump; AirControl which affects how much directional control the player has while airborne; BrakingDecelerationWalking which determines how quickly the character slows when input stops; and bOrientRotationToMovement which, when true, makes the mesh face the current movement direction. These properties are configured typically in the character constructor, and they dramatically change player feel. A common misconception is that movement feels 'laggy' because of input binding; often the issue is a low MaxWalkSpeed, too much braking, or incorrect AirControl settings. Another key detail: you should not multiply movement input by delta time when using AddMovementInput on a character — the movement component applies time scaling internally. Concrete example: setting JumpZVelocity to 600 and AirControl to 0.2 produces a jump with limited mid-air steering, suitable for platforming with predictable arcs. Always test combinations of these properties together — a high MaxWalkSpeed combined with low BrakingDecelerationWalking will feel slippery. Takeaway: tune these knobs iteratively and record DefaultWalkSpeed so sprinting can revert reliably.

When you create AMyPlayerCharacter from the Character base, add UInputAction pointers and function declarations for movement, look, jumping and sprinting. The header typically stores references to your input mapping context and the digital actions for Jump and Sprint. Also add a SprintSpeedMultiplier and a DefaultWalkSpeed field so you can modify MaxWalkSpeed temporarily and revert it. Concretely, declare Move and Look handlers that accept the Enhanced Input value and JumpStarted, JumpCompleted, SprintStarted, SprintCompleted functions for digital events. This separation lets you bind started and completed triggers so sprint ends when the key is released. One misconception to avoid: do not store MaxWalkSpeed in the constructor as the ultimate default; store it in BeginPlay because defaults can change through Blueprints or data assets. Below is the header skeleton used in the lesson content — it declares the properties, functions and the SprintSpeedMultiplier. Use this header as your source of truth when creating the class, and remember that UPROPERTY specifiers control whether you can set these in Blueprints or editor defaults. Creating AMyPlayerCharacter — Header means declare input actions, sprint multiplier, and a defaultwalkspeed field; bind started/completed events later.. In practical terms, define input properties and movement-related fields. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The constructor initializes the capsule size, camera components and the important UCharacterMovementComponent defaults. Typical values shown in the lesson include InitCapsuleSize, bOrientRotationToMovement set true so the mesh follows movement, RotationRate to control turn speed, JumpZVelocity around 600 for a responsive jump, AirControl at 0.2 to allow some mid-air steering, and MaxWalkSpeed defaulting to a comfortable value like 600. There are a few recurring mistakes developers make when implementing character movement. First, enabling both bUseControllerRotationYaw and bOrientRotationToMovement creates a conflict: the character attempts to match controller yaw while also orienting to movement, which results in jerky rotation. Fix this by setting bUseControllerRotationYaw to false when bOrientRotationToMovement is true. Second, not storing DefaultWalkSpeed before modifying MaxWalkSpeed for sprinting causes SprintCompleted to fail to restore the correct speed. Always capture the default in BeginPlay.
